value.overview: The Collared Plover is a small shorebird of the Americas, usually found on open beaches, sandy riverbanks, mudflats, and sparsely vegetated coastal ground. It is compact and brown above with white underparts and a dark breast band. Unlike many familiar North American plovers, it is largely associated with tropical and subtropical regions and is often seen singly or in pairs. In Costa Rica, it is a locally distributed species of suitable Pacific and riverine habitats.
value.classification: The Collared Plover belongs to the plover family Charadriidae in the order Charadriiformes. It was formerly widely treated as Charadrius collaris; many modern taxonomies place it in the genus Anarhynchus.
value.identification: This small plover is about 18 centimeters long. Adults have brown upperparts, white underparts, a dark frontal marking, a dark eye stripe, a chestnut crown and nape, and a prominent black breast band that forms the collar. The bill is short and dark, while the legs are yellowish. Females can appear slightly browner in the dark areas, but the sexes are generally similar. Juveniles are duller and have less sharply defined dark markings.
value.rangeHabitat: The Collared Plover occurs from central Mexico through Central and South America to Chile and Argentina. It uses open, sparsely vegetated ground near the coast and inland waters, including sandy beaches, estuaries, salt flats, exposed river margins, sandbars, and river islands. In Costa Rica it is recorded mainly in lowland coastal and riverine settings, particularly on the Pacific side, and is included on the country's official bird list. It may also occur around suitable disturbed or human-modified shorelines.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident or only locally mobile across its range rather than a regular long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica it occurs as a breeding species and may shift locally among beaches, estuaries, and exposed riverbanks; records are not limited to the main North American shorebird migration season.
value.breeding: Breeding activity in Costa Rica has been reported from approximately March through June. The nest is a shallow scrape on bare or sparsely covered ground, usually above the high-water or flood line on beaches, riverbanks, sandbars, or islands. A typical clutch contains two well-camouflaged, pale buff eggs marked with brown. Adults may use distraction behavior, including a broken-wing display, to draw predators away from eggs or chicks.
value.dietFeeding: The Collared Plover feeds mainly on small insects and other invertebrates found on the surface of sand, mud, or sparsely vegetated ground. It commonly uses a run-and-pause method: the bird moves quickly, stops to watch or locate prey, and then makes a short peck. In Costa Rica, exposed wet margins of rivers, estuaries, beaches, and mudflats provide important feeding areas.
value.behavior: This species is usually wary and is commonly encountered alone, in pairs, or in small loose groups rather than in large flocks. It spends much of its time walking and running over open ground while searching for prey. When disturbed, it may run or fly a short distance before settling again. During nesting, adults can become more conspicuous and may perform distraction displays near an approaching person or predator.

conservation.populationTrend: No clear evidence of a significant global population decline is reported, although population estimates and regional trends are limited.
